payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
A stream of a song pays two parties, at least in principle. One payment goes to whoever owns the recording. The other goes to the people who wrote the song and their publishers, usually through a collecting society. In Latin America those two halves are counted by different organizations, and for 2024 they describe very different years.

Collecting society

An organization that licenses the use of songs on behalf of their writers and publishers, collects the royalties, and pays them out to its members. Most countries have at least one.

Two reports, one region

IFPI, which represents the recording industry, reported that recorded music revenues in Latin America rose 22.5 percent in 2024, the region's fifteenth consecutive year of growth. Streaming made up 87.8 percent of that revenue, and Brazil, up 21.7 percent, was the fastest-growing market in the global top ten. CISAC, the confederation of authors' societies, reported that the region's music collections rose 3.3 percent that year, to €718 million, in a year when music collections worldwide grew 7.2 percent.

A · Recordings, IFPI

Up 22.5 percent in 2024

Recorded music revenue across the region, reported by the recording industry in US dollars.

B · Songs, CISAC

Up 3.3 percent in 2024

Music royalties collected by the region's authors' societies, reported in euros.

The recording side kept its pace in 2025, up 17.1 percent and again the fastest-growing region in IFPI's report, its sixteenth straight year. The authors' figure for 2025 is the one to watch for in CISAC's next report.

What the gap does not prove

The two figures are not one measurement split in half, and the differences matter before anyone reads a conclusion into them. They are kept in different currencies, so exchange rates alone can pull them apart, and neither report restates the region at constant rates. They also cover different uses. CISAC's music figure includes radio, television, concerts and the background music in shops and bars, where a streaming boom arrives slowly if at all. And a society's digital income depends on licenses and on matching streams to registered works, both of which can trail the streams themselves.

IFPI measures recorded music at trade value in US dollars. CISAC reports collections in euros, and its music figure is one part of the €786 million its members in the region collected across all repertoires.

Neither report tries to explain the difference, and nothing here should be read as an explanation either. What the pair establishes is narrower: the growth figure that travels in headlines about the region describes the recordings.

Where a writer appears in the second number

For a songwriter in the region, the first figure makes the news and the second one pays. A writer shows up in it only through registration: a work lodged with a society, under a name and number the society can match, linked to the recordings that carry it. A song that was never registered cannot pay its writer on that side, however often it streams, because the money waits on a match nobody is in a position to make.

The 2024 gap is the question to put to CISAC's 2025 figures. Should the authors' side catch up, the headline was early rather than wrong; a second year of the same spread would mean the region's growth is reaching the recordings and stopping there.

References

IFPI. "IFPI: Amidst highly competitive market, global recorded music revenues grew 4.8% in 2024." March 19, 2025. ifpi.org

IFPI. "Global Music Report 2026: Global recorded music revenues grow 6.4% as record companies drive innovation." March 18, 2026. ifpi.org

CISAC. "CISAC Global Collections Report 2025." cisac.org

CISAC. "Global Collections Report 2025: Music highlights." November 2025. teosto.fi
payload.title: The other half of the song grew 3.3 percent
